That money should come out of the congressman's personal pocket, not the taxpayer, and plus the fact that that congressman person needs to be investigated. explicit_propositions.text: It is outrageous that a congressperson has engaged in sexual misconduct toward a staff member.
Payouts related to misconduct should come from a congressman's personal pocket, not taxpayers' money.
Congresspeople have paid off victims using tax dollars instead of personal funds.
If the ethics committee finds evidence of misconduct, the congressman should be expelled from Congress.
The proposed legislation requires misconduct payouts to be funded personally by the congressman.
The proposed legislation mandates public disclosure of the congressman's name following a complaint.
Confidentiality agreements currently protect congressmen more than victims.
The proposed legislation makes the requirement retroactive.
If a payout occurs after a complaint, the congressman is presumed guilty.
A second bill would allow victims to sue despite being forced into confidentiality agreements.

assumptions.text: Legislators should uphold higher standards of conduct due to their position of public trust.
Expulsion from Congress is an appropriate consequence for proven ethical violations.
Public exposure of misconduct strengthens accountability and deters future abuse.
Confidentiality agreements in harassment cases inherently favor powerful individuals over vulnerable ones.
Taxpayer-funded settlements undermine democratic integrity and fairness.
Personal financial responsibility increases moral accountability among elected officials.
Victims deserve legal recourse independent of coercive settlement terms.
Presumption of guilt based on payout reflects reasonable inference when transparency is lacking.
Ethics committees are capable and credible institutions for investigating congressional misconduct.
The existence of a formal legislative process enables meaningful reform of systemic power imbalances.
